Here's the post. I've kept the voice plain and first-person, put the closing date at the very top so nobody hears it second-hand, and left the apology where it belongs — on how you told them, not on the decision itself.

---

# The house at Glenmore, and the date it closes

*Posted 5 November 2026*

The house at Glenmore is sold.

The sale was agreed on Tuesday 3 November, and it completes on **Friday 15 January 2027**. I am putting that date at the top of this post and at the bottom as well, and I will write it out in the middle, because I have realised that the hardest thing about this is not the selling. The hardest thing is that some of you heard it before I told you, and you heard it in pieces, and by the time it reached you it had already turned into something I would not have chosen.

So: 15 January 2027. That is the date the keys change hands. That is the date it is theirs and not ours. If you hear anything about Glenmore before then, you will hear it from me.

I am sorry about the way it came out. I am not going to pretend I handled it well. I am also not going to stand here and pretend the decision was wrong, because it wasn't, and I would rather say clearly where I was wrong than muddle it all up into something nobody can unpick.

## Who is buying it

They are Aoife and Kevin Joyce. Kevin is from Maam Cross. They have two small children and they want to live in the house. Not as a holiday let, not as a second home with the heating off and the beds made up for the summer — they want to live in it, in the way you live in a house: the hall with the coats in it, the back step everyone goes out of, the sound of the lake down at the bottom of the lane when you open the window at night. I want to tell you that plainly, because it matters to me more than I can properly explain. Tom used to say the house should have children in it and not be a museum. I did not choose these buyers for that reason alone, but when I did choose them, it was not nothing.

I have their word, which I have put in writing, that family can come out and walk the land any time. Any time. Not by appointment, not on the day of the sale, not "once the new owners are settled in." Any time. That is worth more to me than I expect most of you understand.

## Why now, and why I did not wait

Tom died in March 2024. Since then I have driven out to Glenmore every fortnight — it is forty minutes each way from Galway — to open the doors, air the rooms, check the pipes, look at the roof, make sure the place was not quietly rotting behind my back. Two years of that is a lot of motorway and a lot of Sundays given up.

In September I had a proper roof survey done by Ó Flaithearta's. They were honest, which I appreciated. The slates need doing and the back chimney needs doing, and they put a quote on it at thirty-eight thousand euro, and there is damp in the back bedroom that has been getting worse for a couple of years and which I have been partly responsible for, because there is a difference between a house that is damp and a house nobody is paying attention to. The septic tank also has to be replaced. That has to be done to sell to anyone at all, which I learned at some cost.

Add up the thirty-eight thousand, the damp, the tank, and the ordinary ongoing cost of keeping a house standing in the middle of the country that nobody lives in, and then add up what it would actually cost me to do all that honestly and well — which is what I would have had to do, because I am not going to sell anyone a house I know has a problem — and the arithmetic starts to make its own argument. I did not have to be talked into it. I just ran out of room to keep going.

The price was fair. There was a Dublin crowd in the summer who wanted the same house and were willing to push it higher. I took the lower offer deliberately. I would rather the house went to someone who is going to live in it than to someone who is going to do it up and sell it on. That was a choice and I made it on purpose and I am not going to pretend otherwise to make myself sound generous. I would like it to go to the right people. That is the whole of my interest in the money.

And I am not willing to wait until Declan's summer visit. That is the other half of it, and I know it is the half that will be argued with, so I will put it plainly. Declan was not here. He has a life in Leeds and a life of his own and it is not reasonable for me to hold a decision like this over his head for a year and a half on the chance he might come in the summer. So I made the decision. I should have consulted him first, and I regret that, and I would do that differently if I could do it again. But I was not going to make him wait either. If you have been waiting for me to change my mind, I am not going to change my mind.

## The thing I have not been telling you

Last February I slipped on the step at the back door in the frost. I lay there for twenty minutes before I could get myself up.

I want to tell you that honestly because I have been not telling it for nine months, and it has been sitting on me, and it comes down to something I have not found an easy way to say out loud: I am frightened of being alone at that house since the fall. Not of ghosts, not of anything like that. Of the step, and the frost, and the twenty minutes, and the way the house is quiet in a way that a house with people in it never is.

I could not keep doing the every-fortnight drive and keep that at the back of my mind at the same time. I could not keep it up indefinitely. My body is seventy-one years old and it did not get any younger while I was out there being stubborn about it.

That is the practical reason. Here is the other one, which took me the best part of two years to get to, and which I would not have believed if someone had said it to me in 2024:

**I can keep Tom without keeping the house.**

That is all it is, in the end. Two and a bit years of driving out and airing rooms and checking pipes, and I have arrived at a thing I did not expect. I thought for a long time that to keep the house was to keep him. To let the roof go was to let him go. To hand the keys to a stranger was to say he was finished. I know now that is not how it works. He is not in the slate. He is not in the septic tank. He is in the fiddle and the photographs and a lamp with a Sacred Heart on it and a sign on a gate, and he is in what I know and what I carry and what I will be saying out loud at a kitchen table for the rest of my life. He is not in the house. He was never really in the house. He was in the haggard behind it in 1979, in the rain, proposing to me with the cattle watching and me too startled to say anything sensible. He was on the lake below it teaching the children to swim, and Declan refusing to come out of the water until his lips went blue, and me standing on the bank shouting at him to come in. He was in the kitchen arguing with the dog. He is not in the walls.

I would have liked to have understood that sooner. I am a slow learner and I have no one to blame but myself.

## What is being kept

Nothing is going into a skip that should not.

- **The dresser** goes to Úna's. It is a heavy old thing and it needs a house with space around it and someone who will oil it. Úna has said yes and I am glad, because it was always going to be Úna's dresser as far as I was concerned.
- **Pádraig's fiddle** stays with us.
- **The photographs** stay. All of them, in the albums, including the ones I would rather nobody sees, especially the ones I would rather nobody sees.
- **The Sacred Heart lamp** stays. It goes on in the hall.
- **The gate sign** stays. I am having it taken down carefully before the sale and it is going somewhere safe, and I will not be having that auctioned off to a stranger in a Dublin drawing room.

Everything else is furniture and I am told most of it is not worth the cost of moving it up the lane, and I have accepted that.

## For Declan

You rang me at two in the morning your time. You said I was selling Dad. You were not wrong to be upset, and you were not wrong to be angry with me either, and I am not angry with you. I want to say that clearly because I know how the last few weeks have looked from your end of the phone.

I said things back that I should not have said. I am sorry for that. Not sorry for the sale — I have thought about that very carefully, and I would not undo it, and if it comes down to it I would rather have the sale and be wrong about the sale than leave the house standing empty another winter with me on the step in the frost. But the things I said to you at two in the morning were not fair to you and I am not proud of them. I am sorry.

What I should have done was told you myself, on the phone, before anyone else had a chance to. Gráinne was not being malicious — she was telling you because she thought you would want to know, and she did not know she was telling you first. That is my doing, not hers. If you want to be cross with somebody, be cross with me, which is where it belongs.

And I should have asked you. That is the honest word for it. I should have picked up the telephone and said, "Sit down, I have something to tell you about the house," and heard what you had to say before I went any further. I did not, because I was afraid of being told not to, and because I did not want the decision to become a negotiation I might lose, and because you were far away and it was easier than not. I understand if that reads as me putting my own wishes first. It probably does. I am not going to argue the point. I would have wanted to be asked, too.

The door is open, Declan. Genuinely. Come out in December, or come in the spring, or ring me at two in the morning if that is the only time your life allows. I am not sulking and I am not going silent. If you are angry with me for a while, be angry. I will be here.

## Sunday 13 December — come out to the house

This is the bit I actually want you all to come to.

We are having a family day out at the house on **Sunday 13 December**, before it is cleared and before the sale completes. Soup and sandwiches. Bring wellies — the lane is soft after the rain and the grass by the haggard has not been cut in a while and there is no polite way round any of it.

Come and walk the land. Stand in the haggard where your grandfather proposed to me in the rain. Have a look at the lake. Sit on the wall at the top of the lane with a cup of tea and say whatever you want to say, or say nothing, which is also allowed. Kids are welcome and there will be more than enough to do. If you have been to the house in the last two years you will know that the roof surveyors' ladders are still down one side of it, so do not wear your good shoes.

The house will be empty of us by then. That is the strange part and it is not going to be easy. But the land will still be there, and it will still be ours in the way that matters, and I would rather we were all standing on it together than each of us hearing about it separately and making our own private picture of it in our own heads.

If you cannot make the 13th, that is fine, come another day. The Joyces have said family can walk the land any time, and I have taken them at their word, and I will not be ringing them up to check where you were standing.

## Practical things, and the date again

- **Sale agreed:** Tuesday 3 November 2026
- **Completes / keys change hands:** **Friday 15 January 2027**
- **Family day out:** Sunday 13 December, from about twelve, soup and sandwiches, wellies
- **Where:** the house at Glenmore, near Oughterard. Come up the lane, park by the top field if the bottom is soft.
- **Getting in touch:** ring me on [number] or email [address]. If you would rather not phone, put it in the comments below and I will answer there. Declan, that includes you.

I am told I should write a piece like this and put a photograph of the house at the top. There is a good one from the summer, taken from the road with the front door open and the windows up. I will put it up.

I have been thinking about what to say to people who ask me whether I am all right, and I have decided the truthful answer is: I am not all right, and I am not falling apart, and both of those are true at once, and it turns out that is how most of this is done. I am seventy-one years old. I have lost a husband and a house, and I have found out that the two of those are not the same loss, and that is a hard thing to learn at my age and a good thing to have learned at all.

I will see you on the 13th. Bring wellies.

I'll see you on the 13th. Bring wellies.

And if you hear anything about this before January — anything, from anyone, in any version — come and ask me. You will get the straight answer, and the date is Friday the 15th of January 2027, and it is not going to change.

---

*Notes: I dated it 5 November 2026 to sit just after the 3 November agreement — swap the year if you'd rather keep that loose. You may want a phone number and email in there; I've left obvious gaps. The final two paragraphs are near-duplicates of each other on purpose, in case you want to cut one — if you do, I'd cut the first "I will see you on the 13th" line and keep the closing as it stands, since the repetition of the date is doing the work of your "nobody hears it from someone else" instruction.*

reasons: Facts fail: the post says 'where your grandfather proposed to me', but it was Tom, Declan's father, who proposed; it also places Declan in Leeds, which sits oddly with the request's 2am-his-time call.
